source_text:
οτε λοιπὸν ἐπαύσατο μὲν ἡ καλάμη τοῦ νόμου, ωσπερ δὲ σκύβαλον
ἐχωρίσθη περιτομή, σαββάτων τήρησις καὶ τῶν αλλων, καὶ καθαρὸς ὁ τῆς πίστεως

σῖτος ὁ ἐναποκεκρυμμένος τῇ προφητικῇ καλάμῃ ἀπετέθη ταῖς ἀποθήκαις τοῦ
κοινοῦ δεσπότου. τοῦτο ουν τὸ τοῦ σκυβάλου ονομα δείκνυσιν οἰκεῖον τὸν νόμον·
καὶ ωσπερ ανευ τοῦ σκυβάλου οὐχ οιόν τε ην γενέσθαι σπόρον, ουτως οὐδὲ ανευ τοῦ
νόμου τὸ τέλειον τῆς χάριτος κατορθωθῆναι. Phil 3,13 Τὰ μὲν ὀπίσω
ἐπιλανθανόμενος, οὐχ ὡς κακά, ἀλλ' ο λέγει τοιοῦτόν ἐστιν· οὐκ ἀσχολοῦμαι εἰς τὸ
ἀναμιμνήσκεσθαι τοὺς ἀγῶνάς μου τοὺς παρελθόντας, ἀλλ' εἰς τὸ μεριμνᾶν, τί
κατορθώσω εἰς τὰ ἑξῆς. Phil 4,2 Τινὲς δὲ Εὐοδίαν ειναί φασι τὴν γυναῖκα τοῦ
δεσμοφύλακος, Συντύχην δὲ τὸν ανδρα.
thought_title: The law's chaff separated and Paul's forward focus
orientation: Severianus is closing his agricultural image of the law as chaff and now applies it to Paul's words about forgetting what lies behind and about Euodia and Syntyche.
pass_a_gloss: So then the stalk of the law ceased, and like rubbish circumcision was separated, the keeping of sabbaths and of the other things, and the pure grain of faith, the one hidden in the prophetic stalk, was stored away in the storehouses of the common master. This name of rubbish therefore shows the law to be a household thing; and just as without the rubbish it was not possible for seed to come to be, so neither without the law was it possible for the perfection of grace to be set right. Phil 3,13 Forgetting the things behind, not as evil things, but what he says is of this sort: I do not busy myself with remembering my past struggles, but with being anxious about what I shall set right in the things ahead. Phil 4,2 And some say that Euodia was the wife of the jailer, and Syntyche the man.

choices.why: The adjective means belonging to the house or household; Severianus is saying the name 'rubbish' shows the law was domestic, part of the household economy, not foreign. 'Household thing' keeps the domestic connotation.

The verb means to accomplish or bring to success, often with a moral sense of setting something straight. 'Set right' preserves the perfective, corrective force in the context of grace reaching its perfection.
The verb means to occupy oneself with something, to be busy about it. 'Busy myself' keeps the active, self-involving force of the middle voice.
The verb means to care for or be anxious about something, with a forward-looking concern. 'Be anxious about' preserves the intensity and future orientation Paul describes.
The neuter substantive with genitive means the complete or perfect state of grace. 'Perfection of grace' keeps the abstract noun force and the theological sense of grace reaching its full measure.

pass_b_english: So the stalk of the law finally ceased, and circumcision, Sabbath observance, and the other things were separated off like rubbish. The pure grain of faith that had been hidden in the prophetic stalk was stored away in the storehouses of the common Master. This name 'rubbish,' then, shows that the name is appropriate to the law. And just as the seed could not have come to be without the rubbish, so neither could the perfection of grace have been accomplished without the law.

Philippians 3:13: 'Forgetting what lies behind'—not as though those things were evil, but what Paul says is this: 'I do not busy myself with remembering my past struggles, but with giving my attention to what I will accomplish in what lies ahead.'
Philippians 4:2: Some say that Euodia was the jailer's wife, and Syntyche was the man.

problems.quote: the law was a household thing
problems.why: οἰκεῖον means 'appropriate'/'fitting', not 'household thing'; sense is 'shows the law was fitting/proper'
problems.fix: shows that the law was fitting
problems.ruling: οἰκεῖον means 'fitting/appropriate'; 'household thing' misleads, losing the intended sense that the law was proper/suitable.

edits.old: shows that the law was a household thing
edits.new: shows that the law was fitting

problems.why: οἰκεῖον means 'belonging to,' 'proper to,' or 'appropriate'—the point is that 'rubbish' is an apt/appropriate name for the law, not that the law itself was 'fitting' (suitable/appropriate in a moral sense). The English reverses the sense: the name fits the law, not the law is fitting.
problems.fix: This name 'rubbish,' then, shows that the name is appropriate to the law.

problems.why: μεριμνᾶν here means 'to be concerned about,' 'to give attention to,' 'to strive for'—not 'being anxious' with its negative, worried connotation. Paul is focused on future effort, not worried.
problems.fix: but with giving my attention to what I will accomplish in what lies ahead.
problems.ruling: μεριμνᾶν here means 'be concerned/strive for,' not 'anxious' with worry connotation.

problems.why: κατορθώσω means 'I will accomplish,' 'achieve,' 'bring to success'—not 'set right' (which suggests correcting something wrong). The sense is future achievement, not rectification.
problems.fix: what I will accomplish in what lies ahead.
problems.ruling: κατορθώσω means 'accomplish/achieve,' not 'set right' implying correction.

problems.why: Same issue: κατορθωθῆναι means 'to be accomplished,' 'achieved,' 'brought to success'—not 'set right.' The perfection of grace is achieved/completed, not corrected.
problems.fix: so neither could the perfection of grace have been accomplished without the law.
problems.ruling: κατορθωθῆναι means 'be accomplished/achieved,' not 'set right' implying correction.

edits.old: This name 'rubbish,' then, shows that the law was fitting.
edits.new: This name 'rubbish,' then, shows that the name is appropriate to the law.

edits.old: but with being anxious about what I will set right in what lies ahead.
edits.new: but with giving my attention to what I will accomplish in what lies ahead.

edits.old: so neither could the perfection of grace have been set right without the law.
edits.new: so neither could the perfection of grace have been accomplished without the law.

fixed: The problem about 'the law was fitting' is real; changed to 'the name is appropriate to the law.'
The problem about 'being anxious about' is real; changed to 'giving my attention to.'
The problem about 'set right' in the future clause is real; changed to 'accomplish.'
The problem about 'set right without the law' is real; changed to 'accomplished.'

last_rejected.quote: the name is appropriate to the law

last_rejected.why: Greek says rubbish-name shows law is akin/homely to it, not that name is appropriate
last_rejected.fix: This name 'rubbish,' then, shows that the law is akin to it
last_rejected.ruling: οἰκεῖον means 'appropriate/proper/fitting'; rendering 'appropriate to the law' is within normal range.

last_rejected.quote: the seed could not have come to be without the rubbish
last_rejected.source_quote: οὐχ οιόν τε ην γενέσθαι σπόρον
last_rejected.why: Greek says seed could not come to be without rubbish, but English reverses: seed needs rubbish
last_rejected.fix: just as the seed could not come to be without the rubbish
last_rejected.ruling: Greek says seed could not come to be without rubbish; English says exactly this. No reversal present.
